new_statements.quote: ACCENT. — Une particularité de la langue d'Ibôko est que l'accent, outre l'élévation de la voix, comporte le plus souvent un prolongement, une lenteur de prononciation, ce qui fait de la syllabe accentuée une syllabe très longue. Ainsi : môtou se prononce môôôtou. L'accent tombe ordinairement sur la pénultième. Ex. djâla s'asseoir, djalâka assieds-toi. Il tombe aussi quelquefois sur la dernière syllabe, mais la raison en est que le radical n'a qu'une syllabe, Ex. mounsè fourmi blanche (mou étant le préfixe de la 8e classe), ou que cette dernière syllabe est le résultat d'une contraction ou tout autre motif.
new_statements.translation: ACCENT. A peculiarity of the Iboko language is that the accent, besides the raising of the voice, most often involves a prolongation, a slowness of pronunciation, which makes the accented syllable a very long syllable. Thus motou is pronounced mooo-tou. The accent ordinarily falls on the penultimate. Ex. djala 'to sit', djalaka 'sit down'. It also sometimes falls on the last syllable, but the reason is that the radical has only one syllable, e.g. mounse 'white ant' (mou being the prefix of the 8th class), or that this last syllable is the result of a contraction or some other cause.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (pitch rise plus conspicuous lengthening) on the penultimate syllable of the word, moving with suffixation (djala -> djalaka); final accent only when a monosyllabic radical follows a class prefix (prefix unaccentable) or when the final syllable arises from contraction.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; Cambier separately marks unaccented long syllables with a macron and combines accent marks with 'grave'/'aigue' voice quality (proto-tonal notation).
new_statements.exceptions: Final-syllable accent when the radical is monosyllabic after a prefix (mou-nse 'fourmi blanche') or when the final syllable results from a contraction 'ou tout autre motif'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms of an 1891 missionary description; 'accent' conflates pitch ('elevation de la voix') and length, i.e. pre-tonological; the penultimate lengthening matches the non-phonemic penult lengthening Motingea 1990: 69 reports for neighbouring Libobi. Language reported nearly extinct by c. 1950 (Van Bulck 1952 apud Meeuwis & Vinck 2003: 285).
new_statements.identity_note: Cambier 1891 describes 'la langue d'Iboko' of Mankanza (Bangala-Station/Nouvelle-Anvers) and the villages Boukoundou, Mondonge, Mpoumbou, Wambala, Mbaka, Ekolangania, Ikele, Ndondo (preface p. V = AA 24: 293); Meeuwis & Vinck 2003: 284-285 and Glottolog (lgcode 'Iboko = Liboko = Boko [bkp]') equate this with boko1263. The other Glottolog ref, Motingea 1990 'Le parler des Mbonji', is a different parler (Ematelosa/Bolombo; Glottolog: 'looks very similar to Boko'); Motingea & Bonzoi 2008: 76 instead group Mbonji with Boloki/Mpundza as 'mangala de la Ngiri' and affiliate Iboko to Lobala, so the Mbonji sketch (which is silent on stress anyway) should not be taken as Iboko. Stapleton 1903's 'Ngala' is Boloki [bkt], not Iboko. Iboko was reported nearly extinct by c. 1950.

sources.note: Cambier pp. 2-3 (= AA 24: 298-299), 'Notions preliminaires: ACCENT': the accent of Iboko ordinarily falls on the penultimate and is realised as raised voice plus marked lengthening (motou -> mooo-tou); it falls on the final syllable only when the radical is monosyllabic after a prefix (mou-nse) or the final results from a contraction; djala vs djalaka shows it tracking the penult under suffixation. Editors' intro pp. 284-285 identifies the language as Iboko = boko/liboko = Ethnologue BKP; De Boeck's typed annotations (pp. 424-431) add nothing on accent.

sources.citation: Stapleton, Walter H. 1903. Comparative Handbook of Congo Languages. Yakusu: BMS / Bolobo: Hannah Wade Printing Press.
sources.note: 'B. On Accent' sec. 8 (pp. 4-5): 'In the Congo languages the main accent falls on the initial syllable of the stem... a secondary and weaker accent falls on the penult.' His 'Ngala' is the Boloki of Mangala/Monsembe ([bkt]), explicitly 'passing over Liboko' -- a neighbouring variety, not Iboko; a conflicting regional generalisation only.
